2. The most common meaning is "in place of" or "instead of": something replaces another thing. When Archelaus becomes king "in place of" his father Herod (Matthew 2:22), he occupies his position. Or when one gives a snake "instead of a" fish (Luke 11:11), it is a replacement.

3. Used for commercial exchange or price: Jesus gives His life "as a ransom" (Matthew 20:28; Mark 10:45), where the word expresses what is exchanged for something else — His life in exchange for our salvation.

4. When it means "because" or "due to", the word shows that something is the reason or cause: "because you did not receive the love of the truth" (2 Thessalonians 2:10).

5. It can mean "for", expressing an intention or destination: "grace for grace" (John 1:16) means a grace that responds to another grace.

6. In return, in recompense: do not repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17; 1 Peter 3:9), that is, do not give evil in return for evil.
G0473.origine: This word comes from a Greek root meaning "face", "in front of". It is related to the idea of opposite position or face-to-face. The Hebrew word תַּחַת (tachat, "under", "in place of") often corresponds to this word in the Greek translation of the Old Testament. As a prefix, ἀντι- enters into compound words to express opposition (ἀντίχριστος, antichrist), reciprocity, or substitution.
G0473.emploi: This word appears about 20 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and Luke. It is particularly frequent in the teachings of Jesus and in the letters of Paul. In Matthew, it denotes political replacement (Archelaus in place of Herod) or exchange in the Law (eye for eye). In Luke, it explains causes (why Zechariah becomes mute) or substitutions (a fish instead of a stone). In the epistles, Paul uses it to express the refusal of vengeance or the exchange of salvation (the ransom given in favor of many). The meaning varies according to the context: sometimes spatial (face to face), sometimes causal (because), sometimes commercial (in exchange for).
G0473.portee: This word helps the reader understand the fundamental exchange of salvation: Jesus gives Himself as a ransom "for" (in place of) us all. It also emphasizes the call to renounce vengeance — not to repay evil "for" evil — because God Himself has established justice. Recognizing that Jesus substituted Himself for us changes our relationship to grace and to love for our neighbor.

sens: Exchange words
Discuss
Conversate
Dialogue
Debate together
G0474.detail:
1. The word literally means "to throw back and forth": just as one throws a ball back and forth, one throws words to each other. It is the image of dialogue where each person speaks in turn. In Luke 24:17, Jesus asks the disciples: "What are you discussing as you walk?" — he asks what topics they are exchanging with each other.
2. It is a conversation where people share their thoughts and feelings. When one "maintains a conversation," one shares what is on their mind, discussing a topic that concerns them.
3. The word suggests an equal dialogue where everyone has a place to speak, unlike a simple monologue or sermon. It is a true exchange, a genuine encounter through words.
G0474.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "anti" means "against, face to face" and "ballô" means "to throw, to cast." The basic image is that of two people throwing something back and forth. Applied to speech, it creates the idea of a dialogued exchange. The word is rare in biblical Greek: it appears only once in the New Testament.
G0474.emploi: The verb is used only once in the New Testament, in Luke 24:17. Jesus, resurrected but not recognized, approaches two disciples who are walking together and discussing among themselves. He asks them: "What are you discussing?" The context shows that these disciples were talking about the death of Jesus and the rumors of his resurrection — they were exchanging their perplexities and questions. The word perfectly suits this kind of serious and concerned conversation.
G0474.portee: This word reminds us that Christian conversation is not a luxury: it is an essential means of sharing our concerns, doubts, and discoveries of faith. When we converse with other believers about what troubles or amazes us in the Gospel, we follow the example of those disciples who walk with the Lord while speaking freely.

sens: to stand in opposition against someone
to express disagreement or hostility
to adopt a position contrary to that of another person
G0475.detail:
1. The word expresses the act of standing in direct opposition against someone: it is to take a position face to face like an adversary. In 2 Timothy 2:25, Paul speaks of those who "oppose" the truth of the Gospel — they are not simply neutral, they actively stand against it.

2. It manifests a disagreement or hostility that can lead to confrontation. The text shows that these opponents are not just passive contradictors: they harden in a hostile position, which requires the servant of God to exercise gentleness and patience to bring them to repentance.

3. The idea also includes the adoption of a contrary position: these adversaries have taken the opposite side of the truth, and they persist in this contradiction.
G0475.origine: The word is composed of three elements: anti- (against), dia- (through, separation), and tithēmi (to place, to set). The image is that of someone who stands against another person, separating them from themselves. It is a Greek verb formed to express active and deliberate opposition.
G0475.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:25. Paul uses it to describe those who "oppose" the knowledge of the truth — not as mere skeptics, but as adversaries who actively take a stand against the Gospel. The context shows that these opponents need not aggressive confrontation, but "gentle correction," as there is "hope" that God may grant them repentance. This unique word thus captures the reality of a voluntary and tenacious opposition to divine truth.
G0475.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Gospel does not have unanimous acceptance: there are those who oppose the truth of God, sometimes with determination. But Paul's use of this term, accompanied by the recommendation of gentleness and the hope of repentance, shows that even adversaries are not beyond grace. The believer is called to see these opponents not as irreconcilable enemies, but as individuals whom God can still bring back to the truth through His action.

sens: one who opposes someone in court, opposing party in a lawsuit
one who opposes someone in a hostile or threatening manner
G0476.detail:
1. The adversary in a legal sense: it is the person who sues you or against whom you are being sued in court. In Matthew 5:25 and Luke 12:58, Jesus speaks of settling with your adversary before he drags you before the judge and you are thrown into prison — the context is clearly that of a legal dispute, a matter brought before justice. The widow in Luke 18:3 asks the judge to grant her justice against her adversary, someone who wrongs her.
2. The adversary in a general sense: it is any opponent or enemy who threatens or seeks to harm. In 1 Peter 5:8, the apostle calls the devil your adversary — not for a lawsuit, but as a hostile power that prowls and threatens to devour believers. Here, the word takes on a broader and more spiritual meaning.
G0476.origine: The word comes from the preposition "anti" (against) and "dike" (justice, lawsuit, legal action). It literally means one who stands against you in a legal action. The root evokes the idea of opposition, of conflict, originally in a legal framework. In Hebrew, the word often translates "rib," which means quarrel or dispute.
G0476.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. Three occurrences in Luke (12:58 and 18:3) and Matthew (5:25) are words of Jesus about resolving conflicts and obtaining justice: they speak of a real legal dispute. The fourth, in 1 Peter 5:8, applies it figuratively to the devil as the spiritual adversary of Christians. The word thus remains anchored in legal vocabulary, but the Bible expands it to denote any enemy who opposes with hostility.
G0476.portee: These passages remind us that Jesus values reconciliation before open conflict: it is better to settle with your adversary than to let him drag you into court. For the Christian, this means seeking peace rather than nurturing disputes. The application to Satan in 1 Peter 5:8 warns that we have a true spiritual adversary, but also that vigilance and sobriety are our weapons to resist him.

sens: That which opposes, that which contradicts
An assertion that contradicts another
G0477.detail: 1. The word designates what is placed face to face, in contradiction: two things, two ideas that directly oppose each other. In 1 Timothy 6:20, Paul calls the faithful to avoid the "oppositions" of "false science," that is, assertions that contradict and oppose the true knowledge of God.
G0477.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that means "to place": ἀντί ("against") and θέσις ("placement"). The basic image is that of two things placed face to face, in conflict. It is a compound Greek word, forged to express the idea of contradiction or conflict.
G0477.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:20, where Paul exhorts Timothy to guard against the "oppositions of false science." The context shows that it refers to false teachings or assertions contrary to authentic Christian faith. Paul uses this term to designate erroneous doctrines that oppose the true knowledge that God has revealed.
G0477.portee: This word reminds Christians that false doctrine is never neutral: it is an active opposition to the truth of God. Recognizing this opposition allows the believer to remain vigilant against teachings that contradict the Gospel and to preserve the clarity of their faith.

sens: To actively oppose a force, a person, or a trend that seeks to defeat or dominate you
To stand firm in the face of an attack, pressure, or persistent temptation
G0478.detail:
1. The word describes the action of opposing or standing up to something that seeks to defeat us. It suggests an active struggle, not passivity: it is to take a stand against an opposing force. In Hebrews 12:4, believers are urged to "resist to the point of shedding blood, striving against sin" — the image is that of a battle: sin attacks, and the Christian must fight it openly, without giving up.
2. The word can also mean "to hold firm" or "to persevere in the face of opposition." It is less about counterattacking than about steadfastness: standing tall when something pushes you to fall. In the same verse in Hebrews, the context of perseverance in faith shows that resisting sin means refusing to yield, despite fatigue and pain.
G0478.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "anti-" (against, facing) and "kathistēmi" (to establish, to make stand). The basic image is that of "standing against" or "placing oneself in front of." In ancient Greek, the passive or intransitive form of the verb indicates more the idea of "to oppose" or "to resist." In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), Hebrew verbs expressing opposition (like קוּם, "to rise against") are translated by words from this same family.
G0478.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 12:4. It is a term of combat and moral perseverance, used in the exhortation to the Hebrews who are undergoing persecution. The believers receiving this letter are invited to consider their struggle against sin as a noble and enduring fight, comparable to that of the heroes of faith listed in the previous chapter. The context emphasizes that this resistance comes at a cost ("to the point of shedding blood"), but that it is worth undertaking.
G0478.portee: This word invites the Christian to a combative and realistic view of their spiritual life: sin is not merely a difficulty to be avoided, but an adversary to be confronted head-on. To resist does not mean to be passive or to avoid temptation, but to actively engage in the fight through prayer, obedience, and dependence on God. It is a call to moral strength and constancy, especially when the path of faith becomes costly.

sens: To invite someone who has already invited you, to return the invitation
To grant someone the equivalent of what they have given, especially hospitality
G0479.detail:
1. The word designates the action of inviting someone to a meal because they have already invited you: it is responding to an invitation with an invitation. In Luke 14:12, Jesus warns against this natural social practice — inviting to dinner those who, in turn, will invite you, which amounts to making a fair exchange where each reciprocates.

2. More broadly, the word expresses the idea of reciprocity: giving back what one has received. It is the principle of social balance, where a favor calls for an equivalent favor, an invite calls for an invite. Jesus invites us to break this cycle by inviting the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind (Luke 14:13-14), that is, those who cannot repay you.
G0479.origine: The Greek word is composed of "anti" (against, in return, again) and "kaleô" (to call, to invite). It evokes the idea of responding to a call with a call, or inviting the one who has invited you. The root "kaleô" is very common in the New Testament to express calling, invitation, or vocation.
G0479.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 14:12, in the discourse where Jesus teaches about true hospitality. Jesus criticizes the practice of inviting to receive an invitation in return — a calculation of personal interest. He contrasts this transactional mentality with generous hospitality towards those who cannot repay. The unique use of the word emphasizes that this specific critique of the social reciprocity system is a particular teaching of Jesus in this context.
G0479.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine their motivations in hospitality and social relationships. Inviting "in return" reflects a logic of equal exchange and mutual benefit, while Jesus calls for selfless generosity, based not on what one can receive but on free service. It is a major lesson on the difference between the justice of the world (I give to you so that you give to me) and the justice of the Kingdom (I give to you without expecting anything in return).

sens: One who opposes, who resists
One who fights against someone
Force, power that rises against
Principle or desire contrary to another
G0480.detail:
1. The word paints the image of someone standing face to face, in a position of opposition. It is one who resists or contradicts: in Luke 21:15, Jesus promises his disciples wisdom "that all your adversaries will not be able to withstand."
2. More broadly, the adversary is an enemy, an opponent in a conflict or controversy. In 1 Corinthians 16:9, Paul speaks of the many "adversaries" who oppose his ministry.
3. The word also designates a hostile power or force that rises against someone. In 2 Thessalonians 2:4, it describes "the adversary" (the Antichrist) who "exalts himself above all that is called God."
4. By extension, it can describe two realities in internal conflict: in Galatians 5:17, "the flesh" and "the Spirit" are "opposed" to one another in the believer, each pulling in a contrary direction.
G0480.origine: The word combines the preposition "anti-" (against, face to face) and the verb "keimai" (to lie down, to be placed). It literally evokes one who is "placed against" or "in front of." In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses several roots to express this idea: "aïab" (to be an enemy), "tsur" (to besiege, to be narrow), "satan" (to oppose, to accuse). The Greek word captures this richness of meaning: it always conveys the idea of active opposition or a hostile position.
G0480.emploi: The word appears about 8 times in the New Testament, almost always in Paul's epistles. It primarily designates the concrete adversaries of Christ or his messengers: the confused Pharisees facing Jesus (Luke 13:17), the enemies of the disciples (Luke 21:15, Philippians 1:28), the opponents of Paul's ministry (1 Corinthians 16:9). The word is also used more theologically: to describe the conflict between the flesh and the Spirit in the believer (Galatians 5:17), or to designate the Antichrist who stands against God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). In each case, it reinforces the idea of a frontal, almost personal opposition.
G0480.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian path is not without resistance. Believers will encounter external adversaries (persecutors, contradictors) and internal ones (the desires of the flesh). But there is nothing surprising about this: Jesus and his apostles all faced opposition. The word invites the Christian to remain vigilant, to rely on God's wisdom in the face of adversaries (as in Luke 21:15), and to recognize that the true battle is not carnal but spiritual (Galatians 5:17).

sens: In front of, directly facing
By extension, in an opposite or contrary position
G0481.detail:
1. The word designates a spatial position: to be directly in front of something or someone. In Acts 20:15, Paul and his companions arrive "vis-à-vis Chios," meaning at the height of this island, facing it across the sea. It is a precise geographical landmark.
2. Figuratively, the word can evoke opposition or confrontation between two things. It etymologically comes from the preposition "anti" (against) and expresses what stands face to face, in direct view.
G0481.origine: The Greek word comes from the preposition ἀντί (anti, "against") and the adjective κρυός or a root expressing direct proximity. It conveys the idea of what is in front of or vis-à-vis. In biblical Hebrew, the Old Testament often uses the word נֶגֶד (negued), which carries the same meaning of "before" or "in front of." The Greek κοινή (the dialect of the New Testament) employs this form for clarity: not "against" (which would be more abstract), but "directly in front of."
G0481.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:15, in the account of Paul's journey to Jerusalem. It is a precise geographical notation: the ship passes vis-à-vis the island of Chios, in the Aegean Sea. This usage shows that the word belongs to the nautical and geographical vocabulary of common Greek. The context is that of a factual description of a maritime route, where the meaning is purely spatial and concrete.
G0481.portee: This word reminds the reader of the historical and geographical reality of Paul's missionary journey. It emphasizes that Acts is not a fanciful narrative, but contains precise and verifiable details. For the believer, this reinforces confidence in the authentic testimony character of the biblical text.

sens: To take or support someone or something by holding it firmly
To come to someone's aid, to provide assistance
To commit to, participate in something good
G0482.detail: 1. The basic meaning of the Greek word unites the idea of "taking" and "holding against oneself": it is a firm grasp, a seizure. When Mary, the mother of Jesus, praises God, she says that He "has helped Israel" (Luke 1:54), which means that God has lifted them up, supported them like one lifts someone who has fallen. 2. In Paul's words in Acts 20:35, the verb denotes the concrete help given to the weak: "we must support the weak," meaning to work to provide for their needs, to hold them up in their difficulties. 3. In 1 Timothy 6:2, when it says that faithful servants "commit themselves" to doing good for their believing masters, the word expresses a resolute commitment, the act of dedicating oneself to a good deed with firmness and loyalty.
G0482.origine: The word is composed of two parts: "anti" (against, in place of) and "lambanō" (to take, to seize). The starting image is that of taking something in place of another, or taking it firmly, hence the idea of help and support. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word regularly translates Hebrew verbs expressing strength and support, such as the one meaning "to be strong" or "to support," which shows that the Bible used it to describe God's help to His people.
G0482.emploi: This verb appears three times in the New Testament. In Luke 1:54, in Mary's Magnificat, it depicts God's action in helping Israel, His servant. In Acts 20:35, Paul uses it to exhort Christians to support the weak through the work of their hands — a practical act of love. In 1 Timothy 6:2, it describes how believing servants are devoted to the good of their Christian masters. In all these cases, the word emphasizes active support, help that manifests through a firm grasp and lasting commitment.
G0482.portee: This word reminds us that Christian help is not vague goodwill, but a resolute grasp, a true support. God Himself "helps" His people — He does not abandon them in their difficulties. For the disciple, this means that helping the weak should not be a passive charity, but an active, firm, and lasting involvement, like that of God. It is a call to faithfulness in brotherly assistance.

sens: To contradict someone by speaking
To oppose an action or a word
To resist a person or their authority
To express disagreement or hostility
To file a complaint or accuse in court
G0483.detail:
1. To contradict someone means to say the opposite of what they affirm. The Sadducees who "say there is no resurrection" oppose the Pharisaic doctrine (Luke 20:27). It is an act of speech that refuses the affirmation of another.
2. To oppose a word or action is to resist its effect or propagation. Paul preached in Antioch; the Jews "opposed what Paul said, contradicting and insulting him" (Acts 13:45). Here the word describes active resistance against a message.
3. To resist someone or their power is to refuse to obey or recognize them. When it is said to Pilate, "Anyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar," one opposes authority (John 19:12).
4. To openly express disagreement or hostility. The child Jesus "will cause the fall of many": many will oppose Him, meaning they will publicly show their rejection (Luke 2:34).
5. To file a complaint or accuse in court. When Paul says, "the Jews opposed him," he means they presented an accusation against him before the authorities (Acts 28:19).
G0483.origine: The Greek word ἀντιλέγω (antilegō) is composed of ἀντι- (anti-, "against") and λέγω (legō, "to say"). Literally, it means "to say against." This verb inherits the basic image: to place one's word in front of another's, in a conflictual manner. It often translates the Hebrew רִיב (rib, "to contend, to plead") and סוּג (sûg, "to turn away"), terms of confrontation and refusal. The composition with ἀντι- makes it a word of active opposition, not passive.
G0483.emploi: The verb ἀντιλέγω appears 9 times in the New Testament, concentrated in Acts and the Gospels. It often describes public opposition to the word of God or to Jesus: the Jews oppose Paul's message in Antioch (Acts 13:45), and this opposition becomes a sect fought everywhere (Acts 28:22). The word also has a legal sense: to file a complaint (Acts 28:19). In Titus, it refers to resistance to apostolic teaching (Titus 1:9, 2:9). In the Gospels, Luke uses it to express the rejection of Jesus (Luke 2:34; Luke 20:27). The political context clearly appears when one opposes imperial authority (John 19:12). The word always suggests explicit opposition, manifested by word or action.
G0483.portee: This word reveals that the Gospel provokes real and open opposition: Jesus and His messengers should expect to be contradicted and fought against, not universally acclaimed. This opposition is not accidental, but part of the divine plan: Simeon predicts that Jesus "will cause the fall of many" (Luke 2:34). For the believer, it is an invitation to accept that the proclamation of the Gospel may encounter resistance, and to remain faithful despite it. Finally, this word calls us to examine our own reactions: do we not sometimes oppose the word of God through our attitudes or refusals?

sens: action of relying on someone or something
assistance provided to someone in need
practical and material help provided by deacons in the community
G0484.detail: 1. The word primarily evokes the action of grasping, taking by the hand, or leaning on someone to avoid falling — a very concrete image of someone who comes to lift you up when you are weak. 2. By extension, it refers to any form of help or support given to someone in difficulty: coming to their aid, rescuing them. 3. In the Church, particularly in Paul’s writings, this word designates the gift or ministry of help: the action of taking care of the poor, the sick, the widows, as the deacons did. In 1 Corinthians 12:28, Paul lists the various gifts that God has given to believers — some are apostles, others prophets or teachers — and among these gifts is the one of "help," meaning the practical ministry of those who serve, care for, and relieve the material needs of the assembly.
G0484.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that literally means "to take together" or "to seize" (anti- = "against, in front of" + lambanō = "to take"). In Hellenistic times, particularly in petitions to kings, this term came to designate the help or assistance that could be requested. In the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament), it often translates Hebrew words that express the strength or helping arm of God.
G0484.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 12:28, where Paul speaks of the gifts and ministries established by God in the Church. In this passage, "help" is presented as a particular gift, a ministry recognized alongside that of apostles, prophets, or teachers. Although rarely used, this term expresses something essential to the life of the Church: the importance of those who exercise a practical, humble, and often invisible ministry to relieve the sufferings and concrete needs of brothers and sisters.
G0484.portee: This word reminds the reader that not all gifts are spectacular. The gift of help — taking concrete care of others — is as important as that of the prophets who speak publicly. It invites every Christian to recognize that discreetly serving those who suffer or lack something is to exercise a true gift from God, a true mission in the body of Christ. It is a call to active compassion and practical justice.

sens: Disagreement, dispute between people
Verbal contradiction, contestation of a statement
Revolt, rebellion against authority
Active resistance against someone
G0485.detail:
1. A situation where two people or groups clash, disagreeing on an issue. For example, oaths between men serve to settle disputes (Hebrews 6:16).
2. The act of contesting what is said, denying or rejecting it. When someone superior blesses someone inferior, it cannot be contradicted — no one can deny it (Hebrews 7:7).
3. An open revolt, a refusal to submit to one who has authority. Korah was lost in rebelling against Moses (Jude 1:11).
4. An opposition, hostility directed against a person. Jesus endured the opposition of sinners against himself (Hebrews 12:3).
G0485.origine: The word comes from the verb "antilegô" which literally means "to speak against" ("anti" = against, "legô" = to speak, to say). It is thus primarily a word that opposes, a contradiction. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates the word "rib" which denotes a quarrel, a lawsuit, a dispute. The Greek word emphasizes the idea of a word or position that rises against another.
G0485.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, all in epistles (Hebrews and Jude). In Hebrews 6:16, it refers to the dispute that is settled by oath. In Hebrews 7:7, it has the sense of "possible contestation," of what could be denied or rejected. In Hebrews 12:3, it expresses the hostile opposition of sinners against Jesus. In Jude 1:11, it qualifies Korah's revolt, a serious act of insubordination. The word thus oscillates between verbal disagreement and open rebellion.
G0485.portee: This word reminds us that opposition to God and His messengers is a constant biblical reality. Jesus himself suffered opposition from sinners: this is an encouragement for Christians to persevere despite the contradictions they encounter. But it also warns of the danger of rebellion against the authority that God establishes, as Korah tragically experienced.

sens: To reply to an insult with an insult in turn
To return evil for evil through words
To respond to offenses with verbal vengeance
G0486.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of replying to an insult by insulting the one who insulted us. It is reacting to a verbal aggression with a verbal counterattack of the same type. Jesus is the opposite example: although insulted, "he did not retaliate with insults." 
2. It is a form of vengeance — not physical, but through words — that consists of "returning evil for evil." It expresses the natural desire to retaliate when we are offended, an attitude that the text of 1 Peter 2:23 specifically invites us not to adopt.
G0486.origine: The word combines two elements: the prefix "anti-" (against, in return) and the root "loidoreo" (to insult, to curse). The complete verb thus means "to insult in return." It is a word formed to express the idea of reciprocity in outrage — one returns the insult received, just as one would return a blow for a blow.
G0486.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 2:23, in a passage dedicated to Jesus' patience under suffering. The apostle Peter contrasts what Jesus did not do (return insults for insults) with what he did (entrust himself to the one who judges justly). The context is that of imitating Christ in the face of persecution: first-century Christians, oppressed, are called to follow the example of their Master by refusing verbal vengeance.
G0486.portee: This word challenges Christians on how to react to insults and offenses. In the face of verbal aggression, the natural temptation is to retaliate: this verb precisely names that temptation. By placing it in the context of Christ's example, Scripture offers us another way — that of restraint, trust in God, and renunciation of vengeance. It is a call to self-control and trust in divine justice.

sens: The price paid to free a captive or a slave
The payment offered to redeem someone from death or slavery
The giving of oneself as the price of salvation
G0487.detail:
1. A ransom is the price paid to free someone who is captive or imprisoned — like the money paid to recover a hostage. This is the meaning of the basic Greek word: to pay to obtain the freedom of a person.
2. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is used to denote what redeems, delivering from danger or death. It evokes the idea that life has a price, and that price must be paid for captivity to cease.
3. In 1 Timothy 2:6, Paul uses it to describe what Jesus did: "who gave himself as a ransom for all." Here, Jesus himself is the price of redemption — he gives himself as a sacrifice to free humanity from sin and death.
G0487.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: anti- ("in exchange for," "instead of") and lutron ("ransom," "price of redemption"). This root lutron comes from the verb luo ("to loose," "to free"). The basic image is that of loosing the chains of the captive by paying the required price. In the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew word koper ("ransom," "propitiation") is often rendered by words from this same family.
G0487.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:6. Paul uses it to express the central doctrine of Christian salvation: the death of Jesus, who gave himself, is the price that pays for the freedom of all humans. It is a key theological term, borrowed from the vocabulary of ransom (a well-known practice in antiquity), to show that salvation is not free — it has a cost — and that cost, Jesus bore in our place.
G0487.portee: This word teaches that salvation does not come from an arbitrary decision of God, but from a concrete act of love: Jesus pays the price for our liberation. It invites the believer to grasp that their deliverance from sin cost something — the sacrifice of Christ — and calls them to respond with gratitude and surrender to the one who redeemed them.

sens: To use a measure to respond to another measure
To reciprocate, to give in exchange for what has been received
To treat someone as they have treated you
G0488.detail:
1. The verb evokes the action of measuring a quantity in response to another: if someone gives you grain with a certain measure, you measure it back with the same measure. It is the idea of reciprocity in the action of measuring. In Luke 6:38, Jesus states that you will be measured "with the measure you use" — that is, you will be given back using the same standard you employed.
2. More broadly, the word means to reciprocate, to give or do something in exchange or in reaction to what has been received. The context of Luke 6:38 ("Give, and it will be given to you") shows that this reciprocity is part of a cycle of generosity: if you give, God will return to you beyond measure.
3. Figuratively, it is to treat someone according to how they have treated you — an application of the principle "you will be measured with the measure you use." This is not a threat, but a statement of a spiritual law: your actions have consequences that come back to you.
G0488.origine: The word is composed of the prefix *anti-* ("in return, against") and *metreō* ("to measure"). The family of *metreō* includes "metric," "metronome," and many words denoting measurement. The basic image is that of the physical action of measuring with an instrument; the prefix *anti-* indicates the reverse movement, reciprocity. It is a word formed to express the strong biblical idea of retribution and fair exchange.
G0488.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:38. It is found in a saying of Jesus about generosity, where he describes God's reciprocal judgment: the one who gives generously will receive in return according to the measure they have used. The context shows that Jesus is not speaking of a mechanical punishment, but of benevolent divine action — "a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be put into your lap." The word thus expresses less a threat than a promise of just and generous compensation.
G0488.portee: This saying of Jesus calls the Christian to understand that generosity is never lost: God himself acts as an impartial judge who "measures in return." It encourages giving without calculation, trusting that God never leaves a good deed unrewarded. It also teaches that the principle of divine reciprocity exceeds simple justice: God gives "beyond measure," with abundance. It is a promise of security for those who trust in Providence.

sens: Reward or payment given in exchange for an action or service
Punishment or penalty that corresponds to a wrongdoing
Figuratively, reciprocal exchange, reciprocity between two people
G0489.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a reward or salary that corresponds to something: in 2 Corinthians 6:13, Paul asks his readers to reciprocate, that is, to show him the same affection he has shown them — a reciprocity of love.
2. It can also express a punishment that corresponds justly to a wrongdoing: in Romans 1:27, those who have rejected the natural order receive the wages (the retribution) that their straying deserves — the just and proportionate consequence of their sin.
3. The common idea is that of a reaction proportionate to an action: whether it is good received in return for good given, or evil in return for evil committed.
G0489.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: "anti" (against, in return) and "misthos" (wage, price). The image is that of a payment or remuneration that comes back in response to something — literally what comes alongside something else in an equivalent manner. It is a rare word in the New Testament, formed to express this idea of exchange or reciprocity that balances.
G0489.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always in Paul, and always to express reciprocity. In 2 Corinthians 6:13, it refers to a call for mutual affection — a positive and benevolent context where Paul invites his spiritual children to return his love. In Romans 1:27, the context is dark: those who have violated the natural laws established by God receive the punishment that exactly corresponds to their rebellion. In both cases, the word expresses an equivalence: such action, such consequence or such reaction.
G0489.portee: This word reminds us that God governs the world according to justice: every action has its proportionate reaction, every choice its fruits. For the Christian, it invites reciprocity in love and fraternal exchange, while warning against the reality of divine retribution — that which falls upon sin as well as that which crowns faithfulness.

sens: Major city of Syria, commercial and cosmopolitan capital
City of Pisidia in Asia Minor
G0490G.detail:
1. Antioch of Syria is a major metropolis where the disciples scattered by the persecution of Stephen come to proclaim the Gospel (Acts 11:19). It is here that the first mixed Christian community, composed of converted Jews and Gentiles, is born, and the disciples are first called "Christians" (Acts 11:26). Paul stays there with Barnabas to teach and receives the call of the Holy Spirit to mission (Acts 13:1). It is from Antioch that Paul embarks on his missionary journey (Acts 14:26) and where he confronts Peter over the issue of communal meals between Jews and Gentiles (Galatians 2:11).
2. Another Antioch exists in Pisidia, a region of Asia Minor. Paul preaches there during his first missionary journey (Acts 13:14) and suffers persecution, but the Word progresses nonetheless (Acts 14:19-21).
G0490G.origine: The name comes from Greek culture: "Antiochus" honors King Antiochus I, founder of the Seleucid dynasty that rules over Syria after Alexander the Great. Several cities in the Middle East bear this prestigious name at the time of the New Testament, but two in particular mark the life of the early Church.
G0490G.emploi: Antioch of Syria appears thirteen times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and Galatians. It plays a pivotal role in church history: it is the center of the mission to the Gentiles after Jerusalem and Samaria (Acts 11:20-26), the place of the controversy over the Law and grace that leads to the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:22-23, 35), and the base from which Paul departs for his great missionary journeys. Antioch of Pisidia appears twice (Acts 13:14; 14:21), in the context of the first apostolic journey where Paul speaks in the synagogue.
G0490G.portee: Antioch symbolizes how the Gospel crosses cultural and religious barriers. It is here that God's plan to save the nations truly begins to unfold, independent of the Mosaic Law. This city reminds the reader that the heart of early Christianity is not geographically limited to Jerusalem alone, but wherever the Spirit calls and teaches.

sens: City in Asia Minor (modern Turkey), capital of the region of Pisidia
G0490H.detail: Antioch of Pisidia is an important city in southern Asia Minor, distinct from Antioch of Syria. It is here that Paul and Barnabas go during their first missionary journey (Acts 13:14): they preach in the synagogue on the Sabbath. This visit provokes hostility from the Jews and Gentiles who stone Paul and drag him out of the city (Acts 14:19), thinking they have killed him. Despite this violence, Paul returns with Barnabas to strengthen the disciples (Acts 14:21). Paul remembers these sufferings as among the most severe of his ministry (2 Timothy 3:11).
G0490H.origine: The name "Antioch" comes from Greek and designates several cities founded by the Seleucid dynasty. Antioch of Pisidia was established as a Roman colony, unlike Antioch of Syria which was the capital of the Seleucid kingdom. It is a strategic city on the trade routes of Asia Minor.
G0490H.emploi: The Bible mentions Antioch of Pisidia only in the context of the missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas described in Acts. It appears four times in the New Testament: during the arrival and the first message in the synagogue (Acts 13:14), during the violent persecution (Acts 14:19), during the return to strengthen the church (Acts 14:21), and in the memory Paul keeps of it as a place of suffering for the Gospel (2 Timothy 3:11). This city symbolizes the resistance and violence that the Good News encounters.
G0490H.portee: Antioch of Pisidia reminds the reader that the testimony for Christ is not always well received, and that the early missionaries faced real dangers. Paul experienced persecution, stoning, and hostility there, yet he returned to encourage the disciples. It is a lesson in faithfulness despite opposition and courage in proclaiming the Gospel.

sens: person from the city of Antioch
G0491.detail: 1. Nicolas, one of the seven men chosen to distribute aid to the widows of Jerusalem, is presented as being from Antioch, the great city of Syria (Acts 6:5). This term simply designates a citizen or inhabitant of Antioch, distinct from Jews born in Jerusalem.
G0491.origine: The Greek word Antiocheus is formed from the name Antioch, the city founded in the 3rd century BC in northern Syria. The suffix -eus creates an ethnic adjective: it designates belonging to a place, as one would say today "a Lyonnais" or "a Marseillais." The name Antioch itself comes from the Seleucid king Antiochus.
G0491.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament (Acts 6:5), applied to Nicolas. In this context, it emphasizes that Nicolas was a proselyte, that is, a non-Jew converted to the Jewish faith, coming from distant Antioch. His presence among the seven deacons testifies to the welcome of converts from distant regions in the early Church of Jerusalem.

sens: To pass by someone or something without stopping
To deliberately ignore someone, leaving them to their fate
G0492.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical action of passing by someone or something while taking the same path, but without stopping. It is the movement of one who could intervene but continues on their way: the priest sees the wounded man and "passes by" (Luke 10:31), the Levite does the same (Luke 10:32).
2. By extension, "to pass by" means to deliberately ignore someone in need, leaving them without help despite their distress. It is a gesture of indifference or refusal of responsibility: not stopping is to refuse to see and to help.
G0492.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "anti-" (against, in front), "par-" (alongside, next to) and "erchomai" (to go, to come). The starting image is that of someone walking "beside" and "in front of" someone else, passing by without interaction. This composition expresses the contrast: being in the same place, seeing the person, but continuing on one's way.
G0492.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10). It describes the behavior of the priest and the Levite who see the traveler fallen into the hands of robbers: both "pass by." Jesus uses this word to illustrate religious and legalistic indifference in the face of suffering. It is a gesture of refusal of compassion and help.
G0492.portee: This word exposes the hardness of the religious heart: one can encounter the suffering and reality of someone and choose to ignore it. Jesus highlights that true obedience to God is not in outward observance, but in active mercy toward those who suffer. The contrast with the Samaritan, who stops and acts, shows that the disciple of Jesus must see the need and respond with compassion.

sens: A Christian martyr from the church of Pergamum
G0493.detail: Antipas is a faithful Christian from the city of Pergamum who suffered martyrdom for his faith in Jesus. Christ himself refers to him as "my faithful witness" (Revelation 2:13), acknowledging his courage in remaining committed to the Gospel in a city where idolatry and persecution reign.
G0493.origine: The name Antipas is an abbreviated form of the Greek Antipater, composed of anti- ("against") and pater ("father"). It was a common name in the Greek world.
G0493.emploi: Antipas appears only once in the Bible, in Revelation 2:13. He is mentioned among the seven churches to which Christ addresses his messages. Jesus cites him as an example of faithfulness and courageous testimony, even in the face of death, in a context of religious persecution related to imperial worship and pagan practices in Pergamum.
G0493.portee: Antipas embodies Christian faithfulness unto the ultimate sacrifice. His example reminds the reader that authentic faith is not measured by easy words, but by perseverance in adversity and the willingness to lose everything for Christ.

sens: Fortified city located between Joppa and Caesarea, in Samaria, on the coastal road of Judea
G0494.detail: Antipatris is an ancient Judean city built on the road connecting two major ports: Joppa to the south and Caesarea to the north. It stands in Samaria, a region at the heart of the Promised Land. The Bible mentions it only once, during the apostle Paul's journey under Roman military escort (Acts 23:31).
G0494.origine: The name Antipatris comes from Greek and means "who rivals the father" or "worthy of the father." This city was founded by Herod the Great and named in honor of his father, Antipater. It is a typical Greek city of the Hellenistic world during the New Testament period.
G0494.emploi: Antipatris appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:31. It is mentioned in the account where Paul, arrested in Jerusalem, is handed over to Roman soldiers who transport him by night to this fortified city to ensure his safety before leading him to Governor Felix in Caesarea. This mention testifies to the strategic importance of Antipatris on the roads of Judea during the Roman era.
G0494.portee: This place name reminds us how God watches over His servants even in the midst of trials. Paul, a prisoner and in danger, is safely escorted by pagan soldiers through a land he does not control. It is a subtle illustration of divine providence: God opens a way of salvation when everything seems closed.

sens: on the opposite shore
in front of
across from
G0495.detail:
1. This word denotes the opposite shore of a lake or body of water: a position on the other side. In Luke 8:26, after crossing the Lake of Gennesaret, Jesus and His disciples arrive "facing" Galilee, meaning on the opposite shore.
2. Broadly, it indicates a position directly opposite, in front of something: the idea of separation between two places, with a clear spatial reference. It is the location reached when one crosses over.
G0495.origine: The word comes from two elements: "anti-" (against, opposite) and "pera" (beyond, on the other side). It literally describes "the beyond facing," the position that faces from the other side. It is a locational adverb formed from this compound preposition, common in classical Greek to indicate direction or spatial position.
G0495.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 8:26, to describe the place where Jesus and His disciples land after crossing the lake. It geographically locates the land of the Gerasenes in relation to Galilee. In this context, it serves to orient the reader: after the storm is calmed, they are now "on the other side" of the lake, in a different region.
G0495.portee: This word reminds us that biblical geography is not an empty backdrop: it structures the narratives and marks the transitions from one world to another. Here, arriving "facing" Galilee means entering a Gentile territory, where Jesus will meet the possessed man. The opposite shore is not just a geographical position; it is a space where the Gospel spreads beyond Jewish boundaries.

sens: To stand against someone or something
To actively resist a force or will
To act contrary to what is requested or expected
G0496.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of standing face to face against someone, like two adversaries confronting each other. It is an active, tenacious resistance that opposes head-on. In Acts 7:51, Stephen accuses the Jews of constantly opposing the Holy Spirit: not a passive resistance, but a struggle against the will of God.
2. The word emphasizes the deliberate effort to counter an action or influence. It is not an innocuous refusal, but an obstinacy to go against, to fight what should be welcomed.
3. This opposition takes on a moral hue when it targets the divine will: to resist the Holy Spirit is to rebel against God Himself, choosing one's own path rather than the one God proposes.
G0496.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "anti-" (against) and "piptô" (to fall, to strike). The basic image is that of a force striking against another, coming down in opposition. In Hebrew, this verb sometimes translates words like "meribah" (dispute, quarrel) or roots marking rebellion, showing that it expresses a well-defined and declared hostility.
G0496.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:51. Stephen uses it in his final speech before the Sanhedrin to accuse his accusers of perpetually resisting the Holy Spirit. He characterizes this opposition as a trait of the people: "What your fathers were, so are you." This historical repetition ("always") shows that opposition to God is not accidental, but voluntary and persistent. The martyr context—just before his stoning—gives the word a particular intensity: to refuse the Spirit leads to rejecting even those He sends.
G0496.portee: This word invites the reader to examine their heart: where and how might I oppose God? Not just through acts of open revolt, but through daily and subtle resistance to His will. It is a word of judgment, but also of call: recognizing one's opposition to the Holy Spirit is the first step toward conversion and receiving His grace.

sens: To engage in a military action, an organized struggle against an adversary
To stand in hostile opposition, to oppose with force
G0497.detail: 1. The word literally evokes an army campaigning against an enemy. In Romans 7:23, Paul speaks of "another law" that fights against the law of his understanding: it is like two military forces in open conflict. 2. Figuratively, it refers to any form of resolved and active opposition. Here, the law of sin in our members does not merely coexist with the divine law; it fights against it, assailing it, seeking to overcome it.
G0497.origine: The word is composed of "anti-" (against) and "strateuomai" (to wage war, to deploy an army). The root "stratos" refers to an army in battle formation. It is a strong military image: not just a simple disagreement, but an armed confrontation.
G0497.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 7:23. Paul uses it to describe the inner conflict of the believer: the tension between the desire to do good and the power of sin that dwells in the body. Through this martial expression, he emphasizes that it is not a passive or vague struggle, but a real and intense battle.
G0497.portee: This word helps the reader understand the reality of the spiritual battle Paul describes. It is not merely a moral weakness, but a true inner war where sin organizes to combat our will to live according to God. Recognizing this battle for what it is—an active opposition of evil—helps the Christian not to blame themselves alone, but also to take seriously the power of Christ's grace that can set us free.

sens: To stand against someone or something in combat, to oppose them face to face
To refuse to obey, not to submit to an authority
To hold firm in the face of an attempt or assault
G0498.detail:
1. The verb primarily evokes a military image: taking a position against an enemy in battle. In Acts 18:6, the Jews who make "opposition" to Paul adopt a hostile attitude, they "stand against" him with insults.

2. It more broadly means to refuse authority or the established order. One who "opposes" political authority, according to Romans 13:2, is actually opposing the order that God has put in place. This is failing to obey.

3. The word also describes the resistance that God Himself offers: God "resists the proud" (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5), meaning He stands against them, denies them His grace, and opposes their plans. In James 5:6, the righteous condemned "did not resist you," he did not retaliate, he did not raise his hand against his oppressors.
G0498.origine: The Greek word combines the prefix "anti-" (against) and the verb "tassō" (to arrange, to place). The basic image is that of a soldier standing in military formation against the enemy. This creates the idea of standing against, of opposing head-on. The word translates Hebrew terms like "lûts" (to mock, to oppose) and "nasa" (to lift, to raise).
G0498.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and the apostolic epistles. In Acts 18:6, Paul speaks of those who make opposition, an active hostility. In Paul and Peter, the word takes on a sense of civil and spiritual obedience: "to oppose" the government (Romans 13:2) or the authority of God (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). The context of James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 — where God resists the proud — shows that the word can also describe divine action: God stands against those who refuse to humble themselves. In James 5:6, the negation "did not resist you" emphasizes the patience of the righteous in the face of his persecutors.
G0498.portee: This word calls the believer to humility and obedience. It reminds us that resisting established authority ultimately means resisting God Himself (Romans 13:2). But it also teaches that God takes a stand against pride: the one who submits in humility receives His grace, while the proud experience God's resistance. It is a call to a free submission, born of the knowledge that God governs.

sens: That which strikes back, that which resists or opposes
Copy or reproduction of an original model
The concrete reality, of which a figure was only the shadow or announcement
G0499.detail: 1. The primary meaning, rarely used in biblical Greek, is that of an action that strikes back or a resistance: something that opposes or retaliates. 2. The word then designates a copy or reproduction — like the imprint a seal leaves in wax, or a faithful imitation of an archetype. This is the meaning in Hebrews 9:24, where the earthly sanctuary built by men is only an "imitation" of the true heavenly sanctuary where Christ has entered. 3. Finally, "antitupos" can designate the reality itself, of which an ancient figure was only the reflection or prophetic announcement. In 1 Peter 3:21, the "water" of the New Testament baptism is presented as the concrete reality of which the flood in Noah's time was only the figure or prefiguring shadow.
G0499.origine: The word comes from the root "anti" ("against") and "tupos" ("imprint, figure, model"). Its etymology first evokes a striking back or an opposition, then specialized in the idea of correspondence: that which responds to a model, either as a copy or as a reality corresponding to a prefiguration. This nuance between "copy" and "antitypical reality" is particularly important in the New Testament for understanding the relationship between the Old Testament and the Gospel.
G0499.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:24 and 1 Peter 3:21. In Hebrews, it designates the earthly sanctuary as a mere imitation of the heavenly tabernacle to which Christ has access. In 1 Peter, it describes Christian baptism not as a mere imitation of ancient rituals, but as the concrete reality of which the events of the Old Testament were prefigurations. These two uses show how the New Testament uses this word to mark the transition from shadow to reality, from figure to its fulfillment.
G0499.portee: This word helps the reader understand the link between the Old Testament and the New: the institutions, rites, and events of the Old Testament are not vain, but announcements and shadows that find their reality in Jesus Christ and in the Christian life. The baptism of the Christian is much more than the repetition of an ancient purification; it is the fulfillment of what God prefigured. This perspective transforms our reading of Scripture: it shows us that God was leading His people toward a deeper and truer reality.
